title: Fit a lever set to a bored door: hold the outside lever level while both screws are driven
instruction: Fit the lever set to the door: push the outside lever's spindle and posts through the latch until its rose sits flat on the door, fit the inside lever base over them, then drive both screws with the ratcheting screwdriver while holding the outside lever level.
context: Carpenters fit lever sets when they hang doors, and maintenance workers fit them when they replace worn hardware (O*NET 47-2031: 'Install structures or fixtures, such as windows, frames, floorings, trim, or hardware, using carpenters' hand or power tools'; about 0.7 million carpenters and 1.5 million general maintenance and repair workers in the US). The latch already sits in the door's edge bore. The outside lever's flat spindle and two hollow posts must pass, unseen, through the latch inside a 54 mm bore; the inside lever base goes over them, and two screws through it pull the halves together. Left to hang, the outside half droops in its posts' play and the screws lock it crooked, so the levers sit off level and the latch drags. Kwikset's guide: 'Push up on lever base while tightening screws to keep latch horizontal and centered'; Schlage's: 'Make sure the chassis is straight on the door before tightening the screws'.
setup: Millimetres. x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. 1) Door section: a painted solid-core interior door slab cut to 250.3 (x 100 to 350.3) by 34.9 (1-3/8 in, y) by 250 tall, standing on its bottom edge on a 10 mm steel base plate fixed to the table; its faces are normal to y, centre plane y 0, outside face y -17.4 (right arm's side), inside face +17.4. Its latch edge is at x 350.3, facing +x (away from the robot). Bored to the lever set's template: a 54 (2-1/8 in) cross bore centred x 290, z 120 (2-3/8 in backset) and a 25 (1 in) edge bore. 2) Latch: the set's 2-3/8 in tubular passage latch, already fitted and screwed, bolt standing 13 proud; inside the cross bore its frame has a slot for the spindle's blade at the bore's centre and two holes for the posts, 7.9 across, 19 above and below it. 3) Outside half of a Kwikset-style passage lever set (zinc lever and rose, dark bronze finish): rose 66.7 across, lever 107 long (4-7/32 in), 16 tall, standing 53 off the door (2-3/32 in); behind the rose a flat steel spindle blade 2.5 x 9.5 and two hollow steel posts 6.4 across, 39.9 long, round-nosed, tapped #8-32; about 300 g. It hangs by its posts and blade in a grey steel holder: rose's back face centred (340, -61, 120), spindle toward +y, lever level pointing toward the robot (-x). 4) Inside lever base of the same set (the inside lever itself is fitted afterwards with its set screw and is not part of this task): rose 66.7 across with a 24 x 20 square hub 35 long, a slot for the blade and two holes over the posts' ends; two #8-32 pan-head screws sit in it, heads on its face; about 100 g. It hangs on two pegs of a grey holder through its post holes: back face centred (340, 80, 120), hub toward +y, flats level. 5) Ratcheting screwdriver, #2 Phillips bit, set to drive: 200 overall, handle 100 long with two flats 26 apart (facing +-x), 35 across them, about 150 g. It lies on a narrow blue block under its handle, axis along y, bit tip at (225, 35, 60) pointing -y. Play: the posts sit in the latch's holes with 0.75 mm radial clearance, so an unheld outside half droops about 2 degrees. Both grippers start open at their ready poses. Full collider tables in the README.
scoring: Measured after both grippers have been 30 mm or more from both halves and the screwdriver for 2 s. Terms. Through: the outside half's spindle and posts are through the latch, its hub within 2 mm of the bore's centre. On: the base is over the blade and the posts' ends (its centre within 1.5 mm of the spindle's axis). Seated: the rose's rim is within 0.5 mm of its door face all round. Snug: the screw's head bears on the base and a further turn needs force (two full turns in the simulation). Level: the outside lever's long axis and the base's hub flats are within the stated angle of horizontal; the lever points away from the latch edge. 1.0: both halves on and seated, both screws snug, level within 1.0 degree, both halves at rest. 0.75: as 1.0, except that it is level only within 3.0 degrees, or only one screw is snug. 0.5: both halves on and at least one screw caught on its post's thread. 0.25: the outside half through the latch with its rose within 2 mm of the door. 0: anything else, including a lever pointing toward the latch edge. The order of moves and which hand does what are free. Real trial: a digital angle gauge on the lever's top face and on the hub's flat; a 0.5 mm feeler gauge round each rose's rim; a quarter turn more on each screw must take force; then fit the inside lever and turn each lever to 45 degrees to see the bolt go flush and spring back.
reset_notes: Back out both screws and pull off both halves. Check that the latch bolt springs fully out. Push the screws back into the base until their heads sit on its face. Hang both halves on their holders, levers level, and lay the screwdriver on its block set to drive.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; our model, not PhysX threads. Screw shanks are not simulated: a light spring keeps the base on the posts. The bit drives a screw while its tip is within 1.5 mm of the axis; forward turns count, turns back slip (the ratchet). A caught screw draws the halves together as it turns; two turns make it snug, where a real screw takes about a dozen. At the first snug screw the set is fixed where it is, as hand-tight screws hold it. The latch is fixed; post play and masses are estimates.
